1. Which job does the woman do now?

  • Woman: All the time I was at school I wanted to be a nurse, but my mother worked in a shop and said it wasn’t good to be on your feet all day. She wanted me to be a secretary. I did that for a while after I left college, but I wasn’t very keen on it, so I retrained and now I’m doing what I always wanted to.

2. Where will they meet?

  • Girl: Hi Pip. It’s Angie. I’ll see you outside the café tonight at seven thirty.
  • Boy: Oh, but I don’t know where it is.
  • Girl: It’s easy to find. It’s opposite that new supermarket that’s just opened.
  • Boy: I’m not sure where that is either. I’ll wait for you by the bus station, then we can go to the café together. I’ll know where the new supermarket is then too.

3. What was the boy doing when the phone rang?

  • Girl: What did you do yesterday evening?
  • Boy: Well, I was supposed to look after my four-year-old cousin while my aunt went to the theatre. But I wanted to watch the match on television, so she found someone else. The annoying thing was that the phone rang halfway through, and I missed the best goal. I’d finished all my homework early, too.

4. Which date is Brian’s birthday?

  • Man 1: John, did you know it’s Brian’s birthday next week, his 20th? It’s on the 15th.
  • Man 2: That’s Wednesday, isn’t it? Is he having a party?
  • Man 1: Yes, on the 17th at about eight.
  • Man 2: Oh, next Friday. I hope I get asked.

5. Where is the man?

  • Man: Hello Mary. The train arrived much earlier than I expected. I’m on the platform at the moment. Shall I get a taxi? There shouldn’t be a long queue at this time of day ... OK ... I’ll go and have a drink in the café while I wait for you.

6. Which is the boy’s teacher?

  • Boy: I’ve just started learning the piano. I’ve got a really nice teacher. He’s called Mr Hall.
  • Girl: Oh, I know, he taught me when I was quite young. He’s got a beard and lots of black hair, hasn’t he? I used to be quite frightened of him.
  • Boy: Well, the Mr Hall who teaches me hasn't got much hair and it's grey, but he does have a beard. And wears glasses.
  • Girl: But it is the same man, I’m sure. I was only little when he was teaching me.

7. What did the man receive in the post?

  • Man: Was there any post for me this morning?
  • Woman: Yes, there was. Two letters and a postcard. Here you are.
  • Man: One of the letters is for you. I’m expecting a parcel. Did it come?
  • Woman: Oh yes. I put it over there, look.

8. What time is the flight from New York expected?

  • Woman: Excuse me, I’m waiting for flight 712 from New York. It was supposed to arrive at nine twenty. It’s nine thirty-five now and there’s been no announcement of a delay or anything.
  • Man: I’m sorry, Madam. We’ve just had a message to say it took off an hour and a half late. Arrival time is now ten fifty-five.
  • Woman: That’s too bad. I’ve been here since half past eight and it probably won’t arrive when you say. I expect I’ll be here till midday. That’s a whole morning wasted.
  • Man: I can only apologise, Madam.

Conversation 1: Interview with Andy Wells regarding Theme Parks

  • Interviewer: Good morning. Today we’re going to talk about theme parks and we’re going to hear from Andy Wells who has written a guide to theme parks around the world. Welcome to the programme, Andy.
  • Andy: Hi, it’s good to be here.
  • Interviewer: You really have a dream job, don’t you, Andy? Flying round the world all the time, visiting adventure parks ...
  • Andy: Well, yes, it’s pretty exciting. But it’s really hard work too, you know.
  • Interviewer: I bet. So, what’s the number one theme park in the world?
  • Andy: That all depends what you’re looking for. In terms of numbers, it has to be Magic Kingdom at Disney World in Florida, the most famous theme park. But the most popular park for people who like adventure rides is Cedar Point in Ohio, USA. It has the biggest number of rollercoasters in one park, 17, and three water rides. There are lots of other attractions too. Last year they introduced 50 animatronic dinosaurs. You know, life-size models that move and look real.
  • Interviewer: Cool! Have they got anything lined up for this year?
  • Andy: Yeah, there’s a new rollercoaster called the Gatekeeper. Well, actually it’s not a rollercoaster, it’s a wingcoaster. It’ll be the biggest in the world.
  • Interviewer: What’s a wingcoaster?
  • Andy: With a normal rollercoaster you are sitting on a seat with the track under you. With a wingcoaster the seats kind of stick out at the side so the passengers have nothing below or above them. You feel as if you’re flying.
  • Interviewer: So it’s more frightening?
  • Andy: More exciting! Way more exciting.
  • Interviewer: What other attractions have you seen recently?
  • Andy: I’ve just been to The Wizarding World of Harry Potter at the Islands of Adventure in Orlando, Florida. It’s great! You know those shops that sell magic sweets and things in the Harry Potter books? Well, they have those, just like you’ve imagined. There’s a fantastic tour of Hogwarts School where you meet characters from the books. It’s so well done.
  • Interviewer: Right, sounds interesting. In your book you have a lot of theme parks in Asia too. Can you tell us about them?
  • Andy: Sure. Tokyo has had a Disneyland for quite a long time, which attracts a lot of people. Ocean Park in Hong Kong has also been going for a long time – that has a lot of marine animals as well as rides. Lotte World, a huge park in South Korea, has the world’s biggest indoor theme park. And then there’s Universal Studios in Singapore. That’s expanding with additions to its New York street section. There’s going to be a Sesame Street dark ride. A dark ride’s a ride inside a building.
  • Interviewer: I see. New York in Singapore?
  • Andy: Yeah, it’s weird, but it works. But the place to watch at the moment is China – they’re really expanding. Lots more parks will open in China in the next few years, including another one with dinosaurs in the north, and Ocean Kingdom in the south. That will have the world’s longest roller coaster and tallest Ferris wheel, as well as boat rides and a night-time zoo.
  • Interviewer: Wow, so that’s opening soon?
  • Andy: Yes, this year. I’ll be there!
  • Interviewer: Have a ride for me, then.

Conversation 2: Interview with Geoff, World Heavyweight Champion

  • Journalist: Good evening, Geoff.
  • Geoff: Hi.
  • Journalist: Perhaps you could tell me a bit about your background. Where are you from exactly?
  • Geoff: Well, I was actually born in 1958, up in the north of England. My parents came to live in Britain after the war.
  • Journalist: It sounds great.
  • Geoff: We moved south to London after that. We were completely broke and I did all sorts of odd jobs to try and make money.
  • Journalist: Goodness, how dramatic! But?...
  • Geoff: But I was lucky – I discovered karate.
  • Journalist: Ah! How, exactly?
  • Geoff: There was a school trip – nothing special really – but we went to this sports center and I just thought “That’s for me!”.
  • Journalist: Just like that?
  • Geoff: Yup. Anyway, I started training. I found myself a Japanese coach and things just happened. I found it came naturally to me and I worked my way up till I found myself in Taiwan for the World Championships. That was in 1982.
  • Journalist: And you won?
  • Geoff: Yeah, suddenly I was World Heavyweight Champion. It was great.
  • Journalist: And you were world champion at that weight five times in all?
  • Geoff: Yeah, that’s right.
  • Journalist: And then you retired?
  • Geoff: Well, I didn’t have much choice.
  • Journalist: And now you’ve got others projects on the go all around the country and even abroad?
  • Geoff: Mm...yeah...we’re going from strength to strength.

Conversation 3: Marek and Tanya discussing holiday plans

  • T: Hi, Marek. Are you looking forward to your holiday?
  • M: Oh Tanya, I can’t wait!
  • T: Where is it you’re going? Is it camping on an island somewhere or am I thinking of someone else?
  • M: Well, we were going camping, but my Dad’s just bought a camper van, so we’re going in that instead. It means you can go to other countries without having to get a flight which is good in a way, but actually I always used to enjoy sleeping in a tent.
  • T: Yeah, I know what you mean, but it must be nice getting to see all the scenery along the way. I have to say the flight is my least favourite part of going abroad on holiday.
  • M: Oh I never mind it actually – and the airport can be quite fun sometimes.
  • T: You must be joking! All those people and nothing to do except look round expensive shops. I mean, you always end up buying something you don’t really want, just because there’s nothing else to do.
  • M: Oh, I don’t. Anyway, where you are off to this year? Florida again?
  • T: Well, I’m getting a bit old for Disneyland, Marek, though my little brother would still like it. We’re actually going somewhere new. It’s like a sports camp where you stay with lots of other kids and learn how to do different activities.
  • M: You mean you’re going without your parents?
  • T: Not exactly. I mean they’re there too doing whatever they want – golf in my dad’s case – but you only actually see them at mealtimes.
  • M: Sounds cool. But will you have to look after your little brother?
  • T: No way. They divide you up according to age. He’ll be doing football and swimming and all that, whereas I get to go to water skiing.
  • M: Wow! Doesn’t that cost a fortune?
  • T: Well, quite a bit so I’m just doing it on one of the days. But there’s windsurfing and water polo too.
  • M: I see.

tasks.tapescript:
Talk/Lecture 1

Japan has resumed commercial whaling after a hiatus of over three decades. Commercial whaling was banned in 1986 by an International Whaling Commission (IWC) moratorium. However, Japan withdrew from the IWC in December. Japan's government has promised all whalers will stay within 320 kilometers from its coast. The Japanese fisheries agency set a quota for killing 227 whales every six months. In the first days of resumed whaling, whalers caught two minke whales, which were taken to the northern port of Kushiro. The whale meat was auctioned in Tokyo and sold for record prices. Eager restaurant owners snapped up the meat at prices of up to $140 per kilo.

Japan has engaged in the practice of whaling for centuries. Whale restaurant chef Mitsuo Tani summed up why he thought the return of commercial whaling was important. He said: "A country that does not preserve its food culture has no future." He also promoted the health benefits of whale meat. He said: "It is five times lower in calories than beef, 10 times lower in cholesterol, two times less fat than chicken and it's packed with iron. But abroad, people do not know this." However, Japan's return to whaling has brought international outcry. The Humane Society accused Japan of starting a "new and shocking era of pirate whaling". It added: "This is a sad day for whale protection globally."

Talk/Lecture 2

The United Kingdom has said it is playing its part in striving for a cleaner and greener planet. For the first time since the Industrial Revolution in the 18th and 19th centuries, the UK is being powered more by zero-carbon fuels than fossil fuels. In each of the first five months of 2019, fossil fuels have produced less than half of the UK's electricity. Analysts say a "tipping point" has been reached and the trend of zero-carbon energy sources providing more power than fossil fuels will continue. Power from wind, solar, nuclear and hydro sources outstripped coal and gas-fired generation. A decade ago, three quarters (75.6 per cent) of the UK's electricity came from coal and gas, and only 22.3 per cent was zero carbon.

The switch to more zero-carbon power was described by the UK's energy chief executive as a "key milestone on the journey towards net zero". CEO John Pettigrew said the zero-carbon share should increase to 90 per cent by the 2030s. The UK's Prime Minister Theresa May has made a commitment to reach net zero carbon emissions by 2050. This would make the UK the first major economy to do so. Energy analyst Tom Burke told the BBC: "Today's landmark is a real tribute to technologists. We have cracked technical problems of dealing with climate change." He added: "As we move towards net zero, jobs will be lost in fossil fuel industries and created in low-carbon industries."

Talk/Lecture 3

Astronomers have promoted Saturn as the planet with the most moons. Saturn has overtaken the solar system's largest planet Jupiter as the "king of the moons". The astronomers recently discovered 20 new moons orbiting Saturn, which brings the planet's total number to 82. This edges out Jupiter, with 79 celestial bodies, into second place. Each of the newly-discovered moons is at least 5km in diameter. Seventeen of them orbit Saturn backwards and take more than three years to complete one orbit of Saturn. The astronomers found the moons using the powerful Subaru telescope, located on Hawaii. The research team will now look for moons that are around a kilometer in diameter.

Lead astronomer Dr Scott Sheppard commented on the perceived origins of the new moons. He said: "We don't think they formed with the planet. We think they were captured by the planet in the past." He posited that Saturn sucked in a swirling mixture of gas and dust to form the moons. Dr Sheppard added: "We think these moons interacted with that gas and dust. These were comets or asteroids that happened to be passing by....They were captured into orbits around the planet rather than falling into the planet. We think these are the last remnants of what formed Saturn." The moons will be named in a competition after giants from Gallic, Inuit and Norse mythology.

passage.title: Why Failure Can Fuel Motivation
passage.text:
Most people see failure as something to avoid, a clear sign that a plan has gone wrong. Yet across sports, business, and education, many psychologists argue that setbacks often push people to work harder rather than quietly give up, because the disappointment itself creates a strong desire to fix whatever went wrong. This kind of response is not automatic for everyone. For many, though, failure becomes a starting point rather than a final ending, and understanding why this happens can help students, workers, and athletes turn frustrating moments into genuinely useful lessons.

Consider a young runner who fails to qualify for a regional competition after months of steady training. Instead of quitting the sport, she studies her race times closely and notices that her final lap is consistently the slowest part of every race she runs. She begins ending each practice with a short, demanding sprint, deliberately training the exact weakness her failure had revealed. Within a few months her overall time improves noticeably. Her coach later remarks that the missed qualification taught her more than any earlier victory had, because it pointed directly to one fixable problem rather than a vague sense of not being good enough.

Researchers who study motivation say failure works because it gives clear, specific feedback. Winning a race or acing a test mainly confirms that current habits are working, so there is little obvious reason to change anything at all. Losing, on the other hand, forces a person to ask exactly what went wrong, and that question can sharpen effort in ways vague encouragement simply cannot match. Some experts describe this shift as turning a broad goal, such as 'get better,' into a narrow, specific one, such as 'improve my final lap by three seconds.'

Failure does not motivate everyone in the same way, however. If a person interprets a setback as proof that they simply lack talent, that same experience can lead to giving up rather than trying again. Supportive teachers, coaches, and parents often shape which of these two responses a student develops, since without steady guidance many young people never learn to reinterpret a setback as useful information. When mistakes are treated as private embarrassments to hide, students tend to avoid future risks, but when adults discuss them openly and calmly, students grow far more willing to attempt difficult tasks again.

Because of this, some schools and companies have begun redesigning how they respond to failure. Instead of only rewarding final results, several workplaces now recognize employees who took a reasonable risk and learned something valuable from an unsuccessful project. Teachers in a handful of schools ask students to write short reflections on what a wrong answer revealed about their own thinking. These small changes will not turn every failure into progress, but they create the kind of environment in which setbacks are far more likely to become genuinely useful.

passage.title: Firstborns and Later-Borns: Testing an Old Idea
passage.text:
For more than a century, popular wisdom has insisted that birth order quietly shapes character: firstborns supposedly grow into cautious, responsible leaders, while younger siblings become the rebellious, creative risk-takers of the family. This idea shows up constantly in parenting advice and casual conversation, treated almost as settled fact rather than as a hypothesis. Only in recent decades, however, has the claim been tested with large, carefully controlled studies that could confirm or dismantle it.

The theory traces back largely to Alfred Adler, an early twentieth-century psychologist who argued that a child's position among siblings creates a distinct psychological environment. According to Adler, firstborns briefly enjoy undivided parental attention before being 'dethroned' by a younger sibling, an experience he believed could produce either heightened responsibility or lasting insecurity. Later-born children never experience this loss of exclusive attention, and Adler suggested this made them more inclined to seek novelty and recognition.

When researchers finally gathered data from tens of thousands of families rather than small convenience samples, the picture that emerged was far less tidy than Adler's framework implied. A widely cited 2015 analysis found a real but exceptionally small difference in IQ favoring firstborns. Yet the same analysis found almost no reliable birth-order effect on personality traits such as extraversion once family size and social background were taken into account. In other words, whatever influence birth order has appears far narrower than popular stereotypes suggest.

One explanation for the modest IQ difference draws on what psychologists call resource dilution: parents generally have more time and attention to give a single child than they later have to divide among several. A firstborn, for a period, effectively receives an only child's share of parental conversation before that attention must be split. Because early verbal interaction is closely tied to later vocabulary scores, even a small early advantage can persist, faintly, into adulthood.

Family size complicates this picture, since it is tangled up with birth order in ways that are easy to overlook. Families with many children tend, on average, to have different resources than smaller families. Simply comparing firstborns to later-borns across a population therefore risks confusing the effect of birth order with the effect of household size. Researchers who fail to separate these two variables risk attributing to birth order what is really a difference in family circumstances.

To address this problem, more rigorous studies now compare siblings within the very same family rather than firstborns from one household against later-borns from another. This within-family approach removes shared factors like household income, since siblings raised in one home share both. What these studies repeatedly show is that siblings often differ substantially in personality, but that birth order itself explains only a sliver of that difference. Far more of it comes from each child's own friendships and experiences, factors psychologists group under the label 'non-shared environment.'

None of this means birth order is entirely meaningless, since the small, well-documented IQ effect does appear real. It does suggest, though, that the sweeping personality claims dominating popular culture rest on far shakier evidence than their confidence implies. A younger sibling's future personality, it turns out, is shaped far more by individual experience than by a fixed place in the family lineup.

passage.title: The Economics and Engineering of Solar Power
passage.text:
Barely fifteen years ago, solar power was widely dismissed as a marginal technology, too costly and unreliable to matter beyond niche applications such as remote sensors. That dismissal now looks badly outdated. In many regions, newly built solar installations already generate electricity more cheaply than newly built coal or gas plants, a reversal few analysts predicted a decade ago. What changed was not a single breakthrough but a steady accumulation of manufacturing and engineering improvements.

Much of the price collapse traces to what economists call a learning curve: for every doubling of cumulative panel production, manufacturing costs have tended to fall by a fairly consistent percentage. This pattern was first documented in industries as different as aircraft assembly and semiconductors. Larger factories, more automated production lines, and steady gains in silicon efficiency all fed into this curve simultaneously, without any single company or government engineering the outcome deliberately.

Falling costs alone, however, have not solved solar power's central technical problem. The sun does not shine on demand, and electricity, unlike most commodities, must generally be consumed at nearly the same instant it is produced. Grid operators in regions with heavy solar adoption have grown familiar with what is informally called the duck curve, in which demand stays roughly stable through the day while solar output surges at midday. It then plunges toward evening, precisely when household electricity use rises sharply, and meeting that steep ramp with other sources has proven disruptive to grid planning.

Battery storage is often presented as the obvious fix, and its costs have fallen almost as dramatically as solar panels themselves. Yet deploying batteries at a scale large enough to smooth an entire regional grid remains slower and more capital-intensive than installing panels alone. Some utilities have turned instead to demand response programs, which pay customers to shift electricity use away from peak hours, or to older technologies such as pumped hydro storage.

Critics of rapid solar expansion raise concerns that go beyond intermittency. Mining the lithium, cobalt, and rare-earth elements used in panels and batteries carries its own environmental costs, and large solar farms can require substantial land, occasionally displacing agricultural use or natural habitat. Some economists further argue that government subsidies have distorted investment decisions, channeling capital toward projects that would not be competitive on cost alone without public support, though supporters counter that fossil fuels long received comparable subsidies with far less scrutiny.

Despite these unresolved debates, investment in solar generation has continued to climb year after year, driven partly by climate policy targets and partly by the economics described earlier. Financial analysts increasingly treat intermittency not as a fatal flaw but as an engineering challenge to be solved alongside falling storage costs and more flexible demand. Whether that optimism proves justified will depend less on the panels themselves than on the unglamorous infrastructure built to support them.

Solar power, in short, has already won the argument over cost, but not yet the argument over reliability at full grid scale. Treating it as a simple substitute for fossil fuel plants misunderstands the transition underway. A more accurate picture presents solar as one component within a broader system, whose ultimate success depends on parallel progress in storage, transmission, and the flexibility of electricity demand itself.

passage.title: Efficiency, the Rebound Effect, and the Limits of Green Technology
passage.text:
It seems intuitively obvious that making something more efficient should reduce its environmental footprint: a car that burns less fuel per mile, a bulb that uses less electricity per lumen, ought straightforwardly to lower total energy consumption. This assumption quietly underpins much environmental policy, from fuel-economy standards to appliance labeling schemes. Rarely questioned in public debate, it turns out to rest on shakier ground than most policymakers acknowledge.

Economists have in fact been skeptical of this assumption for well over a century. In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons observed that Britain's coal consumption rose, rather than fell, after steam engines became dramatically more fuel-efficient, since cheaper operation made coal-powered machinery viable for a far wider range of uses. What later became known as the rebound effect suggests that efficiency gains do not always translate into proportional reductions in total resource use, because they simultaneously make consumption cheaper and therefore more attractive.

Contemporary research paints a genuinely mixed picture rather than confirming Jevons at every turn. Some sectors, such as residential heating in wealthy countries, show only modest rebound: households that upgrade insulation tend to save a meaningful share of the energy that improved efficiency would predict. Other sectors show something closer to what researchers term backfire, in which efficiency gains are more than fully offset by increased use, leaving total consumption higher than before the improvement. Which pattern applies in a given case appears to depend heavily on how price-sensitive that particular form of consumption is.

Two distinct mechanisms are usually distinguished within this broader phenomenon. Direct rebound occurs when a good becomes cheaper to use and people simply use more of it, driving a fuel-efficient car further, for instance, precisely because each mile now costs less. Indirect rebound is subtler: money saved through efficiency in one domain often gets redirected toward other, sometimes equally resource-intensive, purchases elsewhere, so that overall environmental savings may not materialize even where direct use does not increase. Isolating this indirect channel empirically remains notoriously difficult.

None of this necessarily implies that efficiency standards are pointless, though some commentators have drawn precisely that conclusion. What the evidence more cautiously suggests is that efficiency alone, unaccompanied by mechanisms that keep the price of resource use from falling, may fail to deliver the reductions its advocates expect. Many economists therefore argue that efficiency regulation works best paired with a price signal, such as a carbon tax, that prevents savings from simply being spent on additional consumption.

Critics of rebound-effect skepticism push back on several fronts. They argue the effect has often been overstated in wealthy economies where demand for basic energy services is largely saturated, so that further efficiency gains genuinely do reduce consumption rather than unlocking new demand. The same critics tend to concede, however, that rebound may matter considerably more in rapidly developing economies, where rising incomes and previously unmet demand leave far more room for cheaper energy to unlock consumption that would not otherwise have occurred.

Read carefully, the rebound literature does not argue that efficiency improvements are worthless, nor does it hand critics of environmental policy an easy dismissal of such measures. It argues something narrower and more demanding: that efficiency should be treated as a necessary but not sufficient condition for reducing environmental harm, one whose benefits depend on the economic context surrounding it rather than on the technology alone.

  • Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R4Q7): Kết hợp các dữ kiện về cơ chế bật nảy và vai trò của giá cả ở các đoạn cuối để suy luận rằng hiệu suất chỉ giảm tác hại môi trường khi giá tài nguyên không bị giảm sâu (hoặc được giữ mức hợp lý qua công cụ thuế/giá).
  • Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính & Mục đích của tác giả (R4Q3, R4Q9): Phân tích lập luận toàn cục của bài đọc:
    • Với R4Q3, tổng hợp thông tin toàn bài để xác định ý chính (các cải tiến hiệu suất có thể bị triệt tiêu một phần do sự gia tăng tiêu dùng ở các khía cạnh khác).
    • Với R4Q9, nhận diện mục đích viết chính của tác giả nhằm lập luận rằng tăng hiệu suất là điều cần thiết nhưng chưa đủ nếu chỉ đứng một mình.

Lời khuyên: Hãy ưu tiên hoàn thành trước các câu hỏi định vị vị trí nhanh như Quy chiếu (R4Q4) và Từ vựng (R4Q2, R4Q8). Tiếp theo, thực hiện đọc quét dữ kiện cho các câu Chi tiết (R4Q1, R4Q5, R4Q10) và câu Loại trừ (R4Q6). Cuối cùng, dựa trên bức tranh thông tin toàn cảnh đã nắm bắt, bạn sẽ dễ dàng xử lý các câu đòi hỏi tính tổng hợp cao gồm Suy luận (R4Q7), Ý chính toàn bài (R4Q3) và Mục đích của tác giả (R4Q9).

questions.question: According to the passage, what did Jevons observe about coal consumption in Britain?
options: It increased after engines became widely available, regardless of fuel efficiency.
It increased slightly after engines improved, though only in select industries.
It decreased after steam engines became more fuel-efficient, confirming expectations.
It increased after steam engines became more fuel-efficient, not as expected.

questions.question: The word "saturated" in paragraph 6 is closest in meaning to _______.
What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Efficiency gains reliably guarantee major cuts in overall resource use.
Efficiency gains never reduce use because increased use always cancels them.
Carbon taxes are the only policy tool that solves the rebound effect.
Efficiency gains may be partly offset by increased consumption elsewhere.

options: Direct rebound means using a good more; indirect means spending savings elsewhere.

options: Rebound may matter more in rapidly developing economies with rising incomes.
Efficiency gains in wealthy economies genuinely reduce consumption, not unlock demand.

The rebound effect is often overstated in wealthy, demand-saturated economies.

options: Price signals fail to work unless efficiency standards are removed first.

options: To celebrate recent breakthroughs in carbon tax legislation worldwide.

options: Few economists believe it works best paired with a carbon tax.

tasks.title:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. You work at a hotel, and a customer has emailed asking about booking a room.

Read part of the customer's email below.
tasks.content:
I'm planning to stay at your hotel next month and would like some more information before I book.

  • What is the room rate, and what rooms are currently available?
  • What facilities does the hotel offer?
  • Could you recommend some activities I could do during my stay?
tasks.description: You should write at least 120 words. You don't need to include your name or addresses. Your response will be evaluated in terms of Task Fulfillment, Organization, Vocabulary and Grammar.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng đề:

Đây là dạng Formal/Semi-formal Email (thư trả lời khách hàng trong môi trường kinh doanh), vì người viết đóng vai nhân viên khách sạn trả lời khách hàng tiềm năng. Đề bài yêu cầu trả lời đủ 3 ý chính: (1) giá phòng và phòng hiện có, (2) các tiện nghi của khách sạn, (3) đề xuất hoạt động cho khách trong thời gian lưu trú. Giọng văn cần lịch sự, chuyên nghiệp nhưng vẫn thân thiện. Bài viết cần tối thiểu 120 từ.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục logic (Organization):

  • Greeting: Chào hỏi lịch sự. Ví dụ: Dear Mr./Ms. [Name],
  • Opening: Cảm ơn khách hàng đã quan tâm. Ví dụ: Thank you for your interest in staying with us. I'm happy to provide the information you requested.
  • Body 1 (giá và phòng hiện có): Ví dụ: We currently have deluxe double rooms available at $80 per night, as well as family suites at $120 per night.
  • Body 2 (tiện nghi): Ví dụ: Our hotel offers a range of facilities, including a swimming pool, a fitness centre, free Wi-Fi, and complimentary breakfast.
  • Body 3 (đề xuất hoạt động): Ví dụ: During your stay, I'd highly recommend visiting the nearby night market and taking a guided tour of the old town.
  • Closing: Ví dụ: Please let us know if you would like to proceed with a booking or if you have any further questions.
  • Sign-off: Best regards, [Your Name].

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):

Dùng thì hiện tại đơn để mô tả thông tin cố định (giá, tiện nghi), và cấu trúc lịch sự (I'd recommend, We currently offer) phù hợp với văn phong kinh doanh. Tránh dùng ngôn ngữ quá suồng sã, và nên trình bày thông tin theo trình tự rõ ràng, dễ theo dõi.

Từ vựng quan trọng:

  • room rate: giá phòng
  • availability: tình trạng còn phòng
  • facilities: tiện nghi
  • complimentary breakfast: bữa sáng miễn phí
  • fitness centre: phòng tập gym
  • guided tour: tour có hướng dẫn viên
  • booking confirmation: xác nhận đặt phòng
  • scenic spot: địa điểm ngắm cảnh

Từ nối (Linking words):

  • In addition: Ngoài ra
  • Furthermore: Hơn nữa
  • As for...: Còn về...
  • Should you have any questions: Nếu bạn có bất kỳ câu hỏi nào
  • Regarding...: Về việc...

Cách diễn đạt cảm xúc:

  • We would be delighted to welcome you: Chúng tôi rất vui được chào đón bạn
  • I'm confident you will enjoy your stay: Tôi tin rằng bạn sẽ có một kỳ nghỉ thú vị
  • Thank you for considering our hotel: Cảm ơn bạn đã cân nhắc khách sạn của chúng tôi

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Bỏ sót một trong ba yêu cầu, đặc biệt là phần đề xuất hoạt động.
  • Dùng văn phong quá thân mật, không phù hợp với bối cảnh kinh doanh.
  • Đưa thông tin giá cả và tiện nghi thiếu cụ thể, chung chung.

5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 2 phút cuối:

  • Đếm lại số từ, đảm bảo đạt tối thiểu 120 từ.
  • Kiểm tra đã trả lời đủ cả 3 ý trong đề chưa.
  • Rà soát giọng văn đã đủ chuyên nghiệp, lịch sự chưa.

6. Tư duy làm bài:

Hãy hình dung mình đang thực sự là nhân viên khách sạn muốn thuyết phục khách hàng đặt phòng, vì vậy thông tin cần rõ ràng, cụ thể và giọng văn cần chuyên nghiệp, nhiệt tình.

tasks.title: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
tasks.content:
The use of mobile phones while driving has become a common practice for many people, allowing them to make calls, send messages or use navigation apps on the go.

While some argue that phones can be useful tools for drivers, others believe that using them behind the wheel poses serious safety risks.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
tasks.description: Write an essay to an educated reader to discuss both views and give your own opinion about using mobile phones while driving. Include reasons and any relevant examples to support your answer. You should write at least 250 words. Your response will be evaluated in terms of Task Fulfilment, Organization, Vocabulary and Grammar.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng bài:

Đây là dạng bài Discussion Essay. Bạn cần thảo luận cả hai mặt của việc sử dụng điện thoại khi lái xe — mặt hữu ích và mặt nguy hiểm — trước khi đưa ra quan điểm cá nhân ở phần kết luận. Lưu ý không chỉ tập trung vào một phía ngay từ đầu. Bài viết cần tối thiểu 250 từ.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục (Organization):

  • Introduction: Giới thiệu vấn đề và nêu định hướng bài viết. Ví dụ: While mobile phones can offer convenience for drivers, their use behind the wheel also raises significant safety concerns.
  • Body 1 (mặt tích cực): Ví dụ: On the one hand, phones can be helpful for navigation and emergency communication, allowing drivers to find their way or seek help quickly if needed.
  • Body 2 (mặt tiêu cực): Ví dụ: On the other hand, using a phone while driving significantly increases the risk of accidents, as it distracts drivers from the road and slows their reaction time.
  • Body 3 (quan điểm cá nhân): Ví dụ: In my opinion, although phones can be useful in certain situations, their potential to cause accidents outweighs their benefits, especially when used for texting or calling.
  • Conclusion: Tóm tắt hai mặt và khẳng định lại quan điểm. Ví dụ: In conclusion, while mobile phones offer certain conveniences, I believe stricter regulations on their use while driving are necessary to ensure road safety.

Mỗi đoạn thân bài nên theo cấu trúc: Topic sentence → Giải thích → Ví dụ minh họa → Kết mini-đoạn, giúp bài viết cân đối và có chiều sâu.

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):

Sử dụng cấu trúc đối lập (on the one hand... on the other hand) để phân chia rõ hai mặt của vấn đề, và các cụm từ thể hiện quan điểm cá nhân (in my opinion, I believe) ở phần cuối. Cần có thesis statement nêu rõ định hướng bài viết ngay từ mở bài.

Từ vựng quan trọng:

  • distracted driving: lái xe mất tập trung
  • reaction time: thời gian phản xạ
  • navigation app: ứng dụng dẫn đường
  • road safety: an toàn giao thông
  • hands-free device: thiết bị rảnh tay
  • traffic accident: tai nạn giao thông
  • strict regulation: quy định nghiêm ngặt
  • emergency situation: tình huống khẩn cấp

Từ nối (Linking words):

  • On the one hand / On the other hand (Đối lập hai mặt): Một mặt / Mặt khác
  • In addition / Moreover (Thêm ý): Hơn nữa
  • However / Nevertheless (Đối lập): Tuy nhiên
  • For example / For instance (Ví dụ): Ví dụ như
  • As a result / Consequently (Nguyên nhân-kết quả): Do đó
  • In conclusion / Overall (Kết luận): Tóm lại

Diễn đạt lại ý (Paraphrasing):

  • using mobile phones while driving: có thể thay bằng "phone use behind the wheel"
  • safety risks: có thể thay bằng "potential hazards"
  • convenience: có thể thay bằng "practicality" hoặc "usefulness"

Cách diễn đạt ý kiến:

  • In my opinion / From my perspective: Theo quan điểm của tôi
  • I would argue that...: Tôi cho rằng...
  • Taking everything into account,...: Xét trên mọi khía cạnh,...

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ tập trung vào một mặt của vấn đề mà bỏ qua mặt còn lại (lỗi nghiêm trọng nhất trong bài Discussion).
  • Không đưa ra quan điểm cá nhân rõ ràng ở phần kết luận.
  • Thiếu ví dụ cụ thể để minh họa cho từng luận điểm.

5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 3–5 phút cuối:

  • Kiểm tra xem đã đạt tối thiểu 250 từ chưa.
  • Đảm bảo đã thảo luận cả hai mặt của vấn đề.
  • Xem lại phần kết luận đã nêu rõ quan điểm cá nhân chưa.

6. Tư duy làm bài:

Hãy trình bày cả hai mặt một cách công bằng trước khi đưa ra quan điểm cá nhân. Sự cân đối và logic trong lập luận là yếu tố then chốt để đạt điểm cao ở dạng bài Discussion.

questions: Do you usually eat alone or with other people? Why?
What type of restaurant do you prefer when eating out?
Which season do you like most in your country?
Has your country ever experienced unusual or extreme weather changes?
How does the weather usually affect your daily activities or mood?
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Phần thi này kéo dài 3 phút với 6 câu hỏi, được giám khảo hỏi trực tiếp theo hình thức hội thoại tự nhiên.
  • Chủ đề A (Ăn ngoài): Ba câu hỏi đầu xoay quanh tần suất ăn ngoài, thói quen ăn cùng ai và loại nhà hàng yêu thích, kiểm tra khả năng mô tả thói quen cá nhân.
  • Chủ đề B (Mùa và thời tiết): Ba câu hỏi sau khai thác mùa yêu thích, những thay đổi thời tiết bất thường và ảnh hưởng của thời tiết đến sinh hoạt hằng ngày.
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm gồm: Độ trôi chảy (Fluency), Từ vựng (Vocabulary), Ngữ pháp (Grammar) và Phát âm (Pronunciation).
  • Nên phân bổ khoảng 25–30 giây cho mỗi câu hỏi, tránh dồn quá nhiều thời gian cho một chủ đề.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Áp dụng cấu trúc Answer – Reason – Example (ARE): trả lời trực tiếp, đưa lý do, sau đó minh họa bằng ví dụ cụ thể.
  • Ví dụ Chủ đề A: "I eat out about twice a week, usually with my friends after class because it's a good way to relax and catch up."
  • Ví dụ Chủ đề B: "My favorite season is autumn because the weather is cool and pleasant, perfect for outdoor activities."
  • Luôn tự hỏi Why?/How? sau mỗi câu trả lời ngắn để mở rộng ý (bắt buộc).
  • Dùng một câu chuyển ý ngắn gọn khi chuyển từ Chủ đề A sang B, ví dụ: "Now, moving on to something related to the weather..." (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Giữ tốc độ nói đều, sử dụng các từ đệm tự nhiên như "well", "actually" để tránh im lặng kéo dài.
  • Về thì: dùng hiện tại đơn khi nói về thói quen ăn uống và mùa yêu thích ("I usually...", "I prefer..."), dùng hiện tại hoàn thành khi nhắc đến trải nghiệm thời tiết bất thường ("We have experienced some unusually heavy rain recently").
  • Nếu quên từ, hãy diễn giải bằng cách mô tả (paraphrase) thay vì dừng lại.
  • Từ vựng Chủ đề A: eat out (ăn ngoài), cozy restaurant (nhà hàng ấm cúng), catch up with (gặp gỡ trò chuyện), affordable price (giá cả phải chăng).
  • Từ vựng Chủ đề B: mild weather (thời tiết ôn hòa), extreme heat (nắng nóng gay gắt), unpredictable (khó lường), seasonal change (sự thay đổi theo mùa).

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • a home-cooked meal (bữa ăn tự nấu tại nhà) — Chủ đề A.
  • dine out (dùng bữa bên ngoài) — Chủ đề A.
  • a wide selection of dishes (đa dạng món ăn) — Chủ đề A.
  • pleasant climate (khí hậu dễ chịu) — Chủ đề B.
  • a sudden change in weather (sự thay đổi thời tiết đột ngột) — Chủ đề B.
  • affect one's mood (ảnh hưởng đến tâm trạng) — Chủ đề B.

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • Actually, – mở đầu ý kiến cá nhân tự nhiên (thực ra thì).
  • In terms of... – giới hạn phạm vi câu trả lời (về mặt...).
  • Apart from that, – bổ sung ý (bên cạnh đó).
  • The main reason is that... – nêu lý do chính.
  • Speaking of... – chuyển chủ đề mượt mà (nói đến...).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "Personally, I prefer eating with friends because meals feel more enjoyable when shared." (Cá nhân tôi thích...) — Chủ đề A.
  • "From my point of view, street food restaurants offer the best value for money." (Theo quan điểm của tôi...) — Chủ đề A.
  • "As far as I'm concerned, extreme weather has become more frequent in recent years." (Theo tôi thì...) — Chủ đề B.

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Trả lời cụt lủn kiểu "Yes" hoặc "Summer" mà không giải thích thêm — đây là lỗi nghiêm trọng nhất.
  • Với Chủ đề A: nhầm lẫn giữa "eat out" và "eat outside", hoặc chỉ liệt kê món ăn mà không nêu lý do thích nhà hàng đó.
  • Với Chủ đề B: nói chung chung về thời tiết mà không đưa ra ví dụ cụ thể về hiện tượng bất thường.
  • Dùng sai thì, ví dụ dùng thì tương lai khi mô tả thói quen hiện tại.

5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Dùng câu chêm: "That's an interesting question, let me think for a moment" để có thêm thời gian.
  • Nếu quên từ vựng cụ thể, hãy mô tả bằng từ đơn giản hơn, ví dụ thay vì "typhoon" có thể nói "a very strong storm with heavy rain and wind".
  • Với Chủ đề A, nếu không nhớ chi tiết, có thể nói chung chung về "a cozy little restaurant near my house" rồi phát triển thêm.
  • Với Chủ đề B, nếu bí ý tưởng, hãy liên hệ đến cách thời tiết ảnh hưởng đến việc đi lại hoặc trang phục hằng ngày.

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Hãy xem đây như một cuộc trò chuyện thân mật, không phải một bài kiểm tra căng thẳng.
  • Khi chuyển từ Chủ đề A sang B, hãy "reset" tâm lý và coi đó là một câu hỏi hoàn toàn mới.
  • Ưu tiên sự tự nhiên và trôi chảy hơn là cố gắng dùng từ vựng học thuật phức tạp.

tasks.situation:
Your family is planning a party to celebrate an important occasion.

You are considering the following options:

  • Option 1: Hold the party at a resort
  • Option 2: Hold the party at a family member's house
  • Option 3: Hold the party at a restaurant

Choose the best option and explain your reasons.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Tình huống: gia đình bạn đang lên kế hoạch tổ chức một buổi tiệc để kỷ niệm một dịp quan trọng.
  • Ba lựa chọn: tổ chức tại khu nghỉ dưỡng (resort), tại nhà một thành viên trong gia đình, và tại nhà hàng.
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm: khả năng phân tích, so sánh và đưa ra kết luận thuyết phục, cùng với Fluency, Vocabulary, Grammar và Pronunciation.
  • Thời gian: 4 phút — khoảng 1 phút chuẩn bị và 3 phút trình bày.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc I-C-E (Introduction – Comparison/Body – End): giới thiệu tình huống, phân tích lần lượt ba lựa chọn, sau đó kết luận và đưa ra lý do.
  • Option 1 (resort): "Holding the party at a resort would create a relaxing atmosphere, but it might be quite expensive and less convenient for elderly family members."
  • Option 2 (nhà thành viên gia đình): "Celebrating at a family member's house feels warm and intimate, and it saves money, though space might be limited for a large gathering."
  • Option 3 (nhà hàng): "A restaurant offers convenience and a wide variety of food, but it may lack the personal touch of a home celebration."
  • Mẹo: luôn neo lập luận vào bối cảnh thực tế của một buổi tụ họp gia đình (bắt buộc).
  • Mẹo: dùng từ nối tương phản như "however", "on the other hand" để chuyển giữa ưu và nhược điểm (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Liên kết ba lựa chọn với nhau thay vì nói tách biệt, ví dụ: "Compared to Option 1, Option 2 feels much more personal and cost-effective."
  • Về thì: dùng câu điều kiện loại 1 khi dự đoán hệ quả ("If we choose the resort, we will need a bigger budget") và hiện tại đơn khi mô tả đặc điểm từng lựa chọn.
  • Paraphrase cụm "celebrate" thành "mark the occasion" hoặc "commemorate" để tránh lặp từ.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • a memorable gathering (buổi tụ họp đáng nhớ).
  • intimate atmosphere (không khí ấm cúng, thân mật).
  • cost-effective (tiết kiệm chi phí).
  • convenient location (địa điểm thuận tiện).
  • personal touch (dấu ấn cá nhân).
  • catering service (dịch vụ ăn uống).

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • On the other hand, – nêu quan điểm đối lập (mặt khác).
  • Compared to..., – so sánh giữa các lựa chọn.
  • Taking everything into account, – tổng kết trước khi kết luận (xét tổng thể).
  • Nevertheless, – nhấn mạnh điểm trái ngược (tuy nhiên).
  • As a result, – nêu hệ quả (kết quả là).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "If it were up to me, I would choose to celebrate at a family member's house because it feels more meaningful." (Nếu là tôi...)
  • "I would strongly recommend the restaurant option for its convenience and variety of food." (Tôi sẽ khuyên...)
  • "In my opinion, the emotional value of a home celebration outweighs the comfort of a resort." (Theo ý kiến của tôi...)

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ khen lựa chọn mình chọn mà không chỉ ra nhược điểm của các lựa chọn còn lại.
  • Lặp đi lặp lại từ "good"/"nice" thay vì dùng tính từ học thuật hơn như "convenient", "memorable".
  • Không đưa ra kết luận rõ ràng ở cuối bài nói.

5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Nếu quên từ vựng chuyên ngành, chuyển hướng sang yếu tố chi phí hoặc không gian để tiếp tục lập luận.
  • Dùng câu chêm: "Let's evaluate this option from a different perspective" để có thêm thời gian suy nghĩ.
  • Nếu bí ý ở một lựa chọn, hãy bình tĩnh chuyển sang phân tích lựa chọn tiếp theo.

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Hãy suy nghĩ như một thành viên thực sự đang lên kế hoạch cho gia đình mình — điều gì thực sự ý nghĩa và khả thi.
  • Đưa ra một vài gợi ý cải thiện ngay cả cho lựa chọn được chọn để thể hiện tư duy phản biện.
  • Sự mạch lạc và logic trong lập luận quan trọng hơn việc dùng từ vựng phức tạp.

followUp: What is the most memorable trip you have ever taken?
If you travel, would you rather go with friends or your family? Why?
When you travel, would you choose a luxury tour or a standard tour?
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Chủ đề: Lợi ích của việc đi du lịch, với 3 nhánh ý chính và 1 nhánh ý cá nhân (gợi ý nhánh thứ 4: giảm căng thẳng, thư giãn tinh thần).
  • Tiêu chí chấm điểm: khả năng phát triển ý mạch lạc theo sơ đồ tư duy, cùng Fluency, Vocabulary, Grammar và Pronunciation.
  • Thời gian: 5 phút; khoảng 3–3.5 phút cho bài nói chính, phần còn lại dành cho câu hỏi follow-up.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc IDEA (Introduction – Detail – Example – Add/wrap up) vì chủ đề mang tính trải nghiệm cá nhân, cần cả lý lẽ lẫn ví dụ thực tế.
  • Ví dụ 1 (mở bài): "Traveling brings countless benefits, from broadening our understanding of the world to enriching our personal growth."
  • Ví dụ 2 (nhánh cá nhân): "Personally, I find that traveling helps me reduce stress and clear my mind after a busy semester."
  • Mẹo: khi nói về từng nhánh ý, hãy đưa ra một ví dụ chuyến đi cụ thể để minh họa thay vì chỉ nói lý thuyết.
  • Mẹo: bám sát sơ đồ tư duy để tránh lan man, không lặp lại ý đã nói (bắt buộc).

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Dùng cụm từ chuyển tiếp mượt mà giữa các nhánh ý, ví dụ "Another benefit worth mentioning is...".
  • Về thì: dùng hiện tại đơn để nêu sự thật/quan điểm chung ("Traveling exposes people to different cultures") và hiện tại hoàn thành để nói về trải nghiệm tích lũy ("I have visited several countries in Southeast Asia").
  • Paraphrase "traveling" bằng "exploring new places" hoặc "going on trips" để tránh lặp từ.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • broaden one's horizons (mở mang tầm nhìn).
  • immerse oneself in a new culture (hòa mình vào nền văn hóa mới).
  • step out of one's comfort zone (bước ra khỏi vùng an toàn).
  • hands-on experience (kinh nghiệm thực tế).
  • unwind and relax (thư giãn và giải tỏa căng thẳng).
  • a once-in-a-lifetime experience (trải nghiệm có một không hai).

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • To begin with, – mở đầu nhánh ý đầu tiên (trước hết).
  • Moreover, – bổ sung ý (hơn nữa).
  • Another point worth noting is... – chuyển sang nhánh ý mới.
  • In addition to that, – mở rộng ý (thêm vào đó).
  • To sum up, – kết luận (tóm lại).

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • "I would say that traveling is one of the most effective ways to learn about the world." (Tôi cho rằng...)
  • "From what I've experienced, exploring new places always teaches me something valuable about myself." (Theo những gì tôi trải nghiệm được...)
  • "It seems to me that traveling with family creates deeper emotional connections than traveling with friends." (Đối với tôi thì có vẻ như...)

4. Gợi ý trả lời câu hỏi follow-up:

  • "What is the most memorable trip you have ever taken?" – Share a short story about a trip that left a strong impression, focusing on what made it special.
  • "If you travel, would you rather go with friends or your family? Why?" – Explain that traveling with family feels more relaxing and meaningful, while trips with friends are more adventurous and fun.
  • "When you travel, would you choose a luxury tour or a standard tour?" – Mention that a standard tour is more budget-friendly and authentic, while a luxury tour offers more comfort.

5. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ liệt kê ý mà không giải thích hoặc cho ví dụ cụ thể.
  • Quên nhánh ý cá nhân — nên chuẩn bị trước một trải nghiệm du lịch thực tế của bản thân.
  • Dành quá nhiều thời gian cho bài nói chính, không còn thời gian trả lời follow-up.

6. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Neo vào một chuyến đi thực tế của bản thân hoặc gia đình khi bí ý.
  • Câu chêm học thuật: "That is a complex issue. If we evaluate it from a societal viewpoint..."
  • Nếu quên từ vựng chuyên ngành du lịch, dùng mô tả đơn giản, ví dụ thay vì "itinerary" có thể nói "a plan of places to visit during a trip".

7. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Suy nghĩ từ góc nhìn thực tế của một người trẻ muốn khám phá thế giới và phát triển bản thân.
  • Sự mạch lạc và logic trong luồng ý là yếu tố then chốt để đạt điểm cao.
  • Đừng cố nhồi nhét từ vựng khó, hãy ưu tiên truyền tải ý tưởng rõ ràng và tự nhiên.
